chicken-drumstick-fried-coated-skin-coat.title: Chicken drumstick, fried, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower part of the thigh, containing meat, skin and a small amount of bone. In this product they are pre‑cooked, then coated and deep‑fried. Both the skin and the coating are edible, giving a crunchy crust and rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken drumsticks are a staple of street food and fast‑food menus because of their convenient size and juiciness.
Coatings can be made from wheat flour, breadcrumbs, cornflakes or spice mixes, influencing taste and texture.
Deep‑frying is usually done at 175‑180 °C, which creates a golden crust while keeping the interior moist.
Chicken is one of the most affordable protein sources worldwide; drumsticks contain more fat than breast meat, making them more flavorful.
In many cuisines drumsticks are served with barbecue, honey‑mustard or spicy chili sauces.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide about 18 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and riboflavin (B2), which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies iron, zinc and phosphorus, essential for blood health and bone strength.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: The skin’s fat includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can support cardiovascular health when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat makes the dish filling, helping to control appetite.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Fried, coated drumsticks can contain up to 250 kcal and 15 g of fat per 100 g, which should be considered in a weight‑controlled diet.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt used in the coating and frying raises sodium levels, a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If the coating is made with wheat flour, the product is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; avoid over‑cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drumsticks are easy to eat with your hands: bite off a piece with skin and coating, then chew the meat. Serve them with sauces (barbecue, mustard, garlic), add to salads, sandwiches or as part of a main dish. The skin can be removed if desired, but it is edible and provides beneficial fats.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked fried drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C, where they retain quality for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Long Island Iced Tea is a strong cocktail made with vodka, gin, white rum, tequila, triple sec, lemon juice and cola. Despite its name, it contains no tea; the color resembles tea, which gives the drink its name.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink originated in the 1970s on Long Island, New York.
The original recipe called for only vodka, gin, rum, tequila, triple sec, lemon juice and cola.
Long Island Iced Tea is often considered one of the strongest cocktails, with about 22 % alcohol by volume.
In the US it is typically served in a highball glass over ice with a lemon wedge.
There are many variations, such as the “Texas Tea” which adds bourbon.

items.title: Taste stimulation
items.content: The combination of sour lemon juice and sweet cola creates a vivid flavor contrast that can lift mood.

items.title: Temporary energy boost
items.content: The high alcohol content may give a short‑term feeling of alertness, though it is not a healthy source of energy.

items.title: High alcohol content
items.content: The cocktail mixes several spirits, making it very strong and increasing the risk of intoxication.

items.title: Impact on liver and heart
items.content: Excessive consumption can strain the liver, raise blood pressure, and cause other cardiovascular issues.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain drugs and reduce their efficacy.

items.title: Not recommended for pregnant or nursing women
items.content: Alcohol may negatively affect fetal development and the quality of breast milk.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: In a shaker combine 15 ml vodka, gin, white rum, tequila and triple sec, add 30 ml fresh lemon juice and 15 ml simple syrup. Pour into a highball glass filled with ice, top with cola and stir gently. Garnish with a lemon wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the individual alcoholic ingredients according to the manufacturers’ guidelines. The mixed cocktail should be served immediately; any leftover can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, though flavor and aroma may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Persimmon (Diospyros kaki) is the edible fruit of the persimmon tree, native to East Asia, the Mediterranean region and parts of the United States. Raw persimmon has a sweet, mildly honeyed flavor and a soft yet slightly crisp texture. The fruit is usually eaten fresh, but it is also used in salads, desserts and beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Persimmon belongs to the ebony family and is a close relative of the oak fruit.
There are over 1,000 persimmon cultivars, varying in taste, color and ripening time.
In Japan, persimmon is a symbol of long life and is often given as a New Year’s gift.
Raw fruits of certain varieties (especially astringent types) contain tannins that make them puckery until fully ripe.
The orange‑red color of persimmon comes from high levels of carotenoids.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Raw persimmon provides more vitamin C than many other fruits, supporting immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of beta‑carotene
items.content: Beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A, promotes eye health and skin integrity.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety and supports a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Beneficial minerals
items.content: Persimmon supplies potassium, magnesium and copper, which help regulate blood pressure, muscle function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in persimmon help neutralize free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to persimmon, manifesting as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Raw persimmon contains a notable amount of natural sugars, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Tannin in unripe fruit
items.content: Unripe persimmons can be astringent due to high tannin levels; consuming large amounts may cause stomach discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the raw persimmon whole after washing it. It can be sliced into cubes for salads, added to smoothies, yogurt, or used in desserts. To reduce astringency, some people soak astringent persimmons in water with a pinch of baking soda.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store persimmons at room temperature until they ripen, then move them to the refrigerator. In the fridge they stay fresh for 1‑2 weeks. Avoid overly humid conditions to prevent mold.
